title: Two-step sign-in and a password manager: set up in ten minutes

audience.who: corporate employees of any department who sign in to work accounts every day
audience.knows: how to sign in with a password and use a smartphone; little or nothing about authenticator apps or password managers
audience.cares_about: not being the account that gets broken into, not getting locked out, and not losing time to IT tickets

outcome: After watching, the viewer can turn on two-step sign-in with an authenticator app, save and generate passwords in a password manager, and knows the exact steps to take if their phone is lost.
through_line: A password alone is one lock someone else can copy; a second step on your phone plus a manager that makes every password unique means a stolen password stops being enough, and backup codes mean a lost phone does not lock you out.

arc_plan.what: a colleague's reused password leaks from another site and someone signs in as them: the recognisable moment where a password alone fails
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: why passwords alone fail (reuse, phishing, leaks)

arc_plan.what: two settings, a few minutes, and a stolen password is no longer enough
turning on two-step sign-in: open account security settings, scan the code with an authenticator app, enter the six-digit code, save the backup codes; every click explained
the password manager: one strong master password, saving an existing login, generating a new unique password and letting the manager fill it
losing the phone: sign in with a backup code, tell IT, move the authenticator to the new phone, remove the old one
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: account recovery when a device is lost

arc_plan.what: a short scenario the viewer decides: what to do first when the phone is gone, or which of two sign-in setups survives a leaked password
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: recovery steps and two-step sign-in

arc_plan.what: back to the opening colleague: the same leaked password, now useless without the code on their phone

must_cover.what: why a password alone fails: reuse across sites, phishing, and leaked password lists
what two-step sign-in adds: something you know plus something you have
setting up an authenticator app step by step: scan the code, confirm the six-digit time-based code
saving backup or recovery codes somewhere safe at setup time
a password manager: one strong master password, saving logins, generating unique passwords, autofill
what to do when the phone is lost: backup code sign-in, report to IT, move or reset the authenticator, remove the old device

must_avoid: real product, app or brand names; every tool is generic
statistics or breach numbers without a source
a teacher's tone or an agenda slide opening
SMS codes presented as equal to an authenticator app without the knowledge sheet saying so
advice that conflicts with a company's own IT policy: point to IT for the policy
example_posture: one running colleague at a work laptop and phone, the same accounts throughout; generic screens (a company sign-in page, a generic authenticator app, a generic password manager) shown click by click
visual_direction: a screencast feel: clean generic software screens, a cursor that moves to each control as it is named, the clicked control highlighted, the phone screen beside the laptop when the code is scanned or typed; a before and after of the leaked password; the recovery steps as a short numbered path
voice_note: a calm colleague sitting next to you at your desk, naming each click as it happens; plain words, no jargon without a one-line meaning, never alarmist.
open_questions: topic mode: no source document; every arc anchor points at the knowledge sheet the fact-finder will build
the company's own IT policy (approved apps, where to store backup codes) is unknown; the video points the viewer to IT
